cls: Radiopharmaceutical - bone-seeking beta-emitting radionuclide (Strontium-89 chloride) for palliation of metastatic bone pain
pharm: Strontium-89 chloride (Sr-89, Metastron) is a calcium analog that, after IV injection, localises selectively in bone mineral - preferentially in osteoblastic metastatic lesions - where its beta emission delivers localised radiation to palliate bone pain. (Non-radioactive strontium chloride is also used topically as a dentin desensitising agent in toothpaste.)
quick: 148 MBq (4 mCi) slow IV, or 1.5-2.2 MBq/kg (40-60 microCi/kg)
Intravenous injection; not related to meals
Contraindicated (Category D) - may cause fetal harm
Excreted partly renally; caution in renal impairment (urinary radioactivity)
Peripheral blood counts (platelets, WBC) at least every 2 weeks; confirm bone metastases first
summary: Strontium chloride as the radiopharmaceutical Strontium-89 chloride (Metastron) is given as a single 148 MBq (4 mCi) slow intravenous injection (or 1.5-2.2 MBq/kg) for the palliation of bone pain from osteoblastic skeletal metastases. As a calcium analog, Sr-89 clears rapidly from blood and concentrates in bone, preferentially in metastatic lesions, where its beta radiation (physical half-life ~50.5 days) provides localised pain relief beginning in about 7-20 days and lasting up to 6 months. The major toxicity is myelosuppression - particularly thrombocytopenia and leucopenia - so peripheral blood counts must be monitored, and bone metastases should be confirmed before treatment. Repeat doses are generally not given more often than every 90 days. The non-radioactive salt (stable strontium chloride) is separately used as a topical desensitising agent in toothpaste for dentin hypersensitivity. The Sr-89 radiopharmaceutical (Metastron) is FDA-approved; handle with radiation-safety precautions.
indications: Relief (palliation) of bone pain in patients with painful skeletal metastases that are confirmed prior to therapy (e.g. metastatic prostate or breast cancer)
(Non-radioactive strontium chloride) topical desensitising agent in toothpaste for dentin hypersensitivity - see pearls

dosage.d: 148 MBq (4 mCi) by slow intravenous injection over 1-2 minutes
dosage.n: Confirm bone metastases before treatment; measure activity in a dose calibrator immediately before use

dosage.d: 1.5-2.2 MBq/kg (40-60 microcurie/kg) body weight by slow IV injection
dosage.n: Alternative to the fixed 148 MBq dose

dosage.d: Repeat dose based on response, symptoms and haematologic status
dosage.t: Generally not more often than every 90 days
dosage.n: Allow bone marrow recovery; recheck blood counts before repeating

admin: Administer by slow intravenous injection over about 1-2 minutes; confirm presence of skeletal metastases before treating
Measure the patient dose in a suitable radioactivity calibration system immediately before administration
Use waterproof gloves and effective radiation shielding when handling; follow radiation-safety and ALARA procedures
Sr-89 is excreted in urine and faeces - counsel on radiation-hygiene measures (hand washing, toilet hygiene) for several days after the dose
Do not administer if platelet or white-cell counts are unacceptably low (e.g. platelets <60,000/microL or WBC <2,400/microL) unless benefit clearly outweighs risk
moa: Strontium behaves as a calcium analog. After intravenous injection, soluble strontium-89 clears rapidly from the blood and is selectively taken up by bone mineral (hydroxyapatite), concentrating preferentially in regions of active osteogenesis such as osteoblastic metastatic lesions, where uptake and retention are several-fold higher than in normal bone. Sr-89 is a pure beta emitter (maximum beta energy ~1.46 MeV; tissue range up to ~8 mm) with a physical half-life of approximately 50.5 days. The localised beta radiation delivered within and around the metastatic deposits is thought to relieve bone pain. The exact mechanism of pain relief is not fully established.

absolute: Pregnancy (Category D) - may cause fetal harm
relative: Severely compromised bone marrow (use only if anticipated benefit outweighs risk)
Platelet count <60,000/microL or white blood cell count <2,400/microL
Very limited life expectancy or no bone-pain palliation goal (use restricted to confirmed metastatic bone disease)
monitor: Peripheral blood counts (platelets and white cells) at least every 2 weeks
Signs of myelosuppression - bleeding, bruising, infection
Transient increase in bone pain (flare) in the first 36-72 hours

preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy (Pregnancy Category D). Strontium-89 chloride may cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman, particularly because of fetal skeletal uptake and radiation exposure. Exclude pregnancy before treatment and counsel on effective contraception.
lact: It is recommended that nursing be discontinued by mothers about to receive intravenous Strontium-89 chloride, because of the potential for radiation exposure of the infant from radioactivity excreted in milk.
renal: Strontium-89 is excreted partly by the kidneys (urinary excretion is greater than faecal). No specific dose adjustment is defined, but use caution in renal impairment and counsel on urinary radiation-hygiene precautions; incontinent patients require special handling of bodily fluids.
hepatic: No specific dosage adjustment for hepatic impairment is described in the labeling; Sr-89 is not hepatically metabolised (it is handled as a calcium analog and incorporated into bone).

major: Concurrent myelosuppressive chemotherapy or wide-field external-beam radiotherapy - additive bone marrow suppression; combine with caution and monitor counts closely
moderate: Calcium-containing agents - as a calcium analog, high calcium intake could theoretically alter strontium bone uptake; clinical significance limited
Other bone-seeking radiopharmaceuticals - avoid overlapping use
minor: No clinically significant cytochrome P450 interactions (not metabolised by CYP enzymes)
interactions.diagnostics: Beta emission limits external imaging; bremsstrahlung imaging is possible but Sr-89 is not used as an imaging agent. Confirm metastases with other modalities (e.g. Tc-99m bone scan) before therapy.

common: Bone marrow suppression - thrombocytopenia and leucopenia (the principal expected toxicity)
Transient flare of bone pain 36-72 hours after injection
Chills and fever (especially with rapid injection / flushing reaction)
serious: Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding (haemorrhage, easy bruising, melaena)
Severe leucopenia with risk of infection/sepsis
Prolonged or cumulative myelosuppression with repeated dosing
Calcium-related cardiac effects with very rapid injection
rare: Long-term theoretical risk of radiation-induced malignancy (animal studies showed bone tumours)
emergency: Neutropenic sepsis (fever with very low white-cell count)

monitoring: Confirm presence of skeletal metastases before treatment
Peripheral blood counts (platelets and white blood cells) at least every 2 weeks; expect platelet nadir around 12-16 weeks
Signs of bleeding, bruising or infection; recovery of counts (typically by ~6 months) before any repeat dose
Bone-pain response and need for repeat dosing (not more often than every 90 days)
Radiation-safety follow-up of excreta in incontinent patients
counsel: This is a radioactive medicine given by injection to ease bone pain from cancer that has spread to the bones; it is not a cure
Your bone pain may briefly get worse for a day or two after the injection before it improves; pain relief usually starts within 1-3 weeks and can last up to 6 months
For several days after the injection your urine is slightly radioactive - wash your hands well after using the toilet, flush twice, and follow any radiation-safety advice you are given
Tell your doctor if you have unusual bleeding, bruising, black stools, fever or signs of infection - your blood counts will be checked regularly
Do not receive this if you are or might be pregnant; stop breastfeeding before treatment
pk: Bone-pain relief usually begins in about 7-20 days after injection
Rapid blood clearance with selective bone localisation within hours; effect builds over 1-3 weeks
Physical half-life ~50.5 days (beta emitter); biological retention prolonged in metastatic bone
Pain palliation may last up to ~6 months
Store in its transportation shield at 15-25 C; expires ~28 days after calibration
pearls: PRIMARY ENTRY is the radiopharmaceutical Strontium-89 chloride (Metastron) for palliation of metastatic bone pain; this radiopharmaceutical IS FDA-approved (the openFDA brand-name lookup for 'metastron' returned no record, so this monograph draws on the FDA-approved Metastron prescribing information via the FDA archive/reputable monographs)

DENTAL USE: non-radioactive (stable) strontium chloride is used as a topical desensitising agent in toothpaste, occluding dentinal tubules to relieve dentin hypersensitivity - a distinct, non-radioactive application from the cancer radiopharmaceutical
Sr-89 is a calcium analog and pure beta emitter (half-life ~50.5 days) that concentrates in osteoblastic metastases - confirm bone metastases before treating

Principal toxicity is myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia, leucopenia) - monitor blood counts at least every 2 weeks; platelet nadir typically at 12-16 weeks; do not repeat more often than every 90 days
A transient bone-pain 'flare' may occur 36-72 hours after injection; counsel patients on this and on urinary radiation-hygiene precautions for several days
missed: Not applicable in the usual sense - Strontium-89 chloride is given as a single intravenous dose administered by a nuclear-medicine/radiation specialist, not a self-administered repeating medication. Repeat doses are scheduled based on response and blood-count recovery, generally no sooner than every 90 days.
overdose: Inadvertent overdosage would increase radiation exposure and the risk and severity of myelosuppression. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with intensive monitoring of blood counts and treatment of cytopenias (platelet/red-cell transfusion, infection control). Encouraging fluid intake may promote renal elimination of unbound strontium; oral calcium-containing agents could theoretically reduce gastrointestinal absorption if relevant.
